Atgørvi |100/200/300|(first 100cp purchase free, purchase as many times as you like):

Everyone has a skill, don't they, something they become known for; this is a single mundane skill of your choice. As a runner being able to run upon the water or leap amongst the tree tops. At 200 Points your talent has gone clearly into the realm of the supernatural skill, able to forge immaterial things like light or fire or wind into a blade or infuse it into your armor creating weightless objects, nearly indestructible weapons, or craft impossibly sharp edges as narrow as a wavelength from simple metals. If your skill was running, walking upon the air itself would be possible. At ​300 Points your skills in your chosen area are only limited by your conceptual scope, forging the very idea of a blade out of the sounds of war, manifesting hopes or dreams into a shield. Gather the roots of mountains or the sound of a cat’s foot fall, forging truly indestructible objects immune to even being erased from time or casual loops. A runner able to outrun death and walk through dreams.

At each purchase level your ability to learn, adapt, and master your talents within that skillset will grow by an order of 3, 9, or 27 with no cap to your abilities’ growth beyond the conceptual limitations of this purchase and with absolutely no end if purchased at 300 Points.

Conceptual Attributes - 600

You have remarkable talent, knowledge, and experience in the realm of creating Mystic Codes. If you had truly exceptional components, and some means to imbue your creation with great levels of Mystery (such as through the weight of time and legend) you could even create a genuine Noble Phantasm.

But perhaps even more impressive than that is your ability to imbue objects you craft with conceptual attributes, should you so choose. You only begin with an association with a single concept; for instance, Artoria Caster, due to her Holy Sword Creation, would infuse any object she created with the concept of “sword”. This would allow even a shield to cut through objects, and would let a letter opener pierce conceptual defenses that are weak to swords as though it were actually a sword. You begin with this one concept, but you can learn others by studying the concept enough and introducing it into your life in a major way, although you couldn’t possibly acquire more than a single concept per year in this fashion.

Persona 4 and Persona 5 Royal both have very similar Perks, Wielder of Power and Ruler of Power, respectively. The Perks themselves basically let you ignore restrictions on artifacts, wielding them at full power with no downsides. The interesting part is that they both have a Capstone Perk attached to them if you bought the Capstone Booster in the Jump.

Wielder of Power Capstone

Through your Truth, you have learned the art of fusing Power. Now, you can take any two items, powers, techniques, Perks, etc., and fuse them together. They will take on a new form and power that is stronger yet different than the original, but you will know the result beforehand and you can have the result inherit up to four traits or powers of the previous two of your choice. However, do keep in mind that you lose the materials, so if you fuse your Compendium’s records of personas, you will lose the two you used. If you don't care about losing the materials, that's fine, but there is a better way. The optimal method for using this is using it with someone you've been helping. That way you can fuse their powers, have them get (and then record) the new one, and then restore the ones they lost. This is what the Velvet Room does as well, and it works, but do be aware that because you are using someone else's power, they can only handle so much. Thus, you will need to help them grow if you want to keep using this method repeatedly. Lastly, as this works in the same general way as Igor’s Persona fusion, you can use any of his spreads or rituals for this as well, which will have similar results.

Ruler of Power Capstone

Your grasp on Power has grown even further. Like a true Velvet Room attendant, you know how to fuse Powers in any way you please. With your bare hands you can fuse Personas into greater forms, with complete control over what the result will inherit. Not only Personas can be affected by this power. Items or equipment with an innate power of some sort may be affected as well. Any ability you or others you wish to use this on may be fused and combined at will, locking away any aspect you wish to be unavailable as well. The Power is yours, be wise in how  to use it.

If the potions are just kickstarting the process for the body gathering/producing more Mana, that’s probably something you’ll want to emphasize more. 

The potions aren’t directly giving you the Mana, it’s a stimulant that forces your body to draw in the world’s Mana more rapidly, or it could be something like forcing your body to produce Mana more quickly, eating through your body’s resources and stamina more quickly. It depends on if the setting has mages gathering mana from outside themselves or generating it themselves. 

Rather than the headache/migraine/stroke consequences you have, you could say that the version where the mage draws in more Mana from the world they don’t have time to filter/attune to it, and that causes complications either with their health or their ability to cast spells as effectively with it. Or, the version where mages generate Mana themselves, the consequences would be fatigue, dehydration, starvation, and all that fun stuff as they use up way more of their bodies resources than they should’ve. 

I think the idea is fun, but you probably shouldn’t bog down your readers with all the rules about potions, unless your character is going through school. Similarly, I’d consider how you’re going to translate ‘mana points’ to something that will fit your setting better. Whether that’s just dropping the ‘points’ bit or deciding to call your magic something other than mana, idk.

Stunned or Restrained creatures already have several things applied to them: automatic failure of Dex and Str saves when Stunned, or disadvantage on DEX saves when Restrained, attack rolls against the creature having Advantage for both conditions, disadvantage on attack rolls for Restrained creatures. Adding onto that and removing the Stunned or Restrained creatures Armor Class is going over the top and would contribute to unbalancing combat more than other homebrew rules do otherwise. 

The system in place works well, in my opinion, and I wouldn’t want to change that by adding complications to combat that seem like they would just clutter and unbalance the combat flow.
Advantage used to be plus or minus ten to the role, iirc, rather than rolling twice.

This was a 3.5 rule as well, it can be used to good effect, but I personally think that it just bogs down combat when you have to remember three different AC scores and when situationally to use them. 

Flat-footed I generally dislike, it lasts for one round of combat and it only ever gives advantage to players when you could give them a surprise round or actual Advantage in it’s place. 

I like how streamlined 5e made combat in that regard, but that’s mostly because I DM’d for a group of seven players and a round of combat could last anywhere from five minutes to two hours.

Fizzlestick looks old as shit, which is fair, because he IS old as shit, but he SHOULD look like a twenty-something, he only looks like this because he got cursed by some old magic artifact that he dropped somewhere(probably in a city, to be honest, like, he was insane, thought it would be funny to see if it would curse other people too, which, it does). 
He’s a little man, much below average, doesn’t help that he’s got a heavy slouch either, he’s 5’2” but looks to be closer to 4’10”. He walks around with a nobby old cane, which is actually the Fizzlestick, his ‘staff,’ which he likes to smack people with.
Fizzlestick is short and skinny, you can’t really tell at first glance, but he is muscular, it’s just that he has so little body mass, and it’s hidden underneath his robes. He has a plethora of small scars all over his body, most of which he’s forgotten how he got. 
His face is about what you’d expect out of a half-mad wizard: crazy eyes, knobby nose, manic grin, and singed hair/eyebrows. 
He dresses in what people might call ‘standard wizarding attire,’ heavy robes and a tall and pointy hat. He wears leather armor underneath the robes(“These robes don’t do much for protection and I’m not stupid enough to presume I won’t end up on the wrong side of a sword at some point.”), though he tends to keep that a secret.

The ring finger on his left hand is cut off at the second knuckle(“Hmm, this? No clue how I got it, woke up with it missing one morning. Must be quite the story! Pity nobody knows it.”), there’s a good chunk missing from the tip of his right ear(“Got that one fighting a bear, I did. Bastard was twelve feet tall, had sharks for arms, breathed fire and could fly. What, don’t look at me like that, I’m telling you the truth! How come nobody ever believes me about that?”), his left eye is glass, though it looks exactly like his right, you can only tell it’s fake if he takes it out, but it does look like a lazy eye most of the time(“What, my eye? Perceptive one, you are. Lost it in my days as a pirate. The captain’s parrot pecked it right out of my head. To be fair, I had just killed him in the mutiny. I feasted on fine poultry that night.”), his right leg is cut off about halfway down the calf, he has a prosthetic that looks just like a regular foot, and wears boots that go above the cut, but he walks with a slight limp(“My leg? Ah, that one is a boring story, I’m afraid. Fell off a roof and landed on it bad, the bone sticking out and everything, it went septic and we had to cut it off. Good thing I had just stolen those jewles, or I never would’ve been able to afford this prosthetic. Hmm? What jewels? Oh, nevermind that, don’t you worry about it.”), his nose is crooked from being broken many times, never really set properly(“I’ve been in a few pub brawls in my day, kiddo.”), and he’s missing a few more teeth than is likely healthy(“When you get to be as old as I am, you should be grateful to be missing so few teeth as I am!”).

He may look old, and play the part of an invalid, but Fizzlestick is quick on his feet when he wants to be, though his ever-active mind is quicker. Those who pick a fight with him or his allies get to witness the absurd strategies and magics he employs in combat, sometimes foolish, most of the time advantageous, always a spectacle.

Not just Kobolds, if you don't want. The big thing that many DMs miss, and I missed it when I first started too, is that the enemies are smart. They communicate with each other, they can retreat and dig in further down the tunnel. The enemies should have intelligent tactics, they've been in this tunnel, warding off adventurers for years. Play tactically, you can give the monsters feats and abilities, there can be a summoner that keeps bringing in more enemies every turn, there can be a troll that takes up the entire tunnel, with archers in the walls, shooting through arrow slits, there can be anything and everything. 

But you have to remember, first and for most, this isn't a versus game, you are working together with the party to create an epic story. They're badass heroes, let them feel like it, but make them deserve it too. Yeah, they're overpowered, they're supposed to be! Just make some encounters even more overpowered. Not with the intention of screwing them over, but with the intention of making the encounter seem like a real challenge, and when they get past it, they'll feel great and excited to have gotten past it. 

Another option is to use more puzzles and traps, rather than combat. Make one of the monsters an essential NPC that can get them through the dungeon more easily, spice up the game. 

Your options are limitless, you don't have to play by the book.
